keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 1324-1359, about 51,600 km2 (gazetteer cells for Gascony plus the Gironde). The 1324 loss of Limousin, Périgord, Quercy and the Agenais is the researcher's reading (confidence 2): the Saint-Sardos page says the forfeiture covered the whole duchy and that the 31 March 1325 truce, which Edward II 'reluctantly ratified', 'involved the tacit recognition of the loss of most of the duchy'; it names neither the Limousin nor the Périgord nor Quercy, and the Agenais only as the price Charles IV asked in December 1324. The Gascon core stayed under English garrisons with a nominal French occupation after the truce ('Charles IV was to be allowed to go into nominal occupation of what was left of the Duchy of Aquitaine'); the page gives no end for it and it is not drawn. No campaign of 1337-1359 is dated on the pages opened.

region.text: Toulouse, captured by William IX and Philippa in 1098

ledger.note: 1098: William IX takes Toulouse. 'He and Philippa did capture Toulouse in 1098, an act for which they were threatened with excommunication', while Raymond IV was away on crusade. Aquitaine is the occupier. The page also has him mortgage 'Toulouse back to Bertrand, the son of Raymond IV' to finance his crusade and says 'In 1122, William lost control of Toulouse, Philippa's dower land, to Alfonso Jordan'; it does not say whether control was interrupted in between, so one span 1098-1122 is drawn (the dates 1098-1100 and c. 1114-1123 are not on the page). region.text: the whole duchy 'officially came under the rule of the French Crown' when Louis VII became king

ledger.note: 1137: Eleanor of Aquitaine marries Louis VII and the duchy passes to the French crown. 'She married Louis, heir to the French throne, three months after her father's death' (William X died 9 April 1137; the wedding was on 25 July 1137, Eleanor of Aquitaine page); 'When Louis VI died, and Eleanor's new husband became King Louis VII, the duchy of Aquitaine officially came under the rule of the French Crown'. The accession date is not on the pages. On 18 May 1152 Eleanor married Henry, 'transferring her Aquitaine lands from Louis to Henry' (Eleanor page), so the land goes to the Angevin Empire in 1152 and is drawn there until 1204. Cliopatria draws these years as Kingdom of France (1139-1151) and Angevin Empire (1152-1204). The vassalage of the duchy under the crown ends in the same year (vassal_end below); kingdom-of-france /ledger/10 puts it in 1138 from Cliopatria's relation row.

region.text: the duchy as held in 1294: 'France then occupied Aquitaine'

ledger.note: 19 May 1294: the French Parlement declares the duchy forfeit and France occupies it. 'The Parlement then declared Edward's fief in Aquitaine forfeit to the Crown on 19 May 1294'; 'France then occupied Aquitaine'. Edward I answered on 24 June 1294 by renouncing his vassalage. The Guyenne page dates the confiscation to 1296 (page conflict; the war page's dated sentence is followed; the occupation's own start is bridged to the forfeiture). France is the occupier of Aquitaine's land. Mirror missing in kingdom-of-france (no 1294 event there).

region.text: Limousin, Périgord, Quercy and the Agenais beyond the Gascon core, the lands of the duchy beyond the Gascon core that the 1325 truce left in French hands ('the tacit recognition of the loss of most of the duchy')

ledger.note: 1324: the War of Saint-Sardos strips the duchy of its periphery. Charles IV 'had already declared the duchy forfeit' (the forfeiture covered the whole duchy); 'In August 1324, Charles of Valois, the king's uncle, invaded Aquitaine' and 'Most towns surrendered immediately'; the Earl of Kent held La Réole until he surrendered on 22 September (infobox: 1 July to 22 September 1324). The truce of 31 March 1325 let the French keep their conquests ('restored only as reparation for a war') and 'involved the tacit recognition of the loss of most of the duchy'. The Guyenne page also says the duchy was confiscated 'in 1296 and 1324'. The region is the researcher's reading: the page does not name the Limousin, Périgord or Quercy, and mentions the Agenais only as the concession Charles IV asked in December 1324. The Duchy page's 'essentially corresponding to Gascony' for 1337 fits the reading. Mirror missing in kingdom-of-france (no 1324 event there).

region.text: Gascony and the Bordelais, the fief Philip VI 'reclaimed' in 1337

ledger.note: 1337: Philip VI reclaims the fief. 'In 1337, King Philip VI of France reclaimed the fief of Aquitaine (essentially corresponding to Gascony)' from Edward III. The vassalage ends here, although the English kept the land in fact; the Brétigny page has the 1360 lands held 'free and clear, without doing homage'. kingdom-of-france /ledger/36 gives May 1337 (Hundred Years' War page, not opened in this pass).

ledger.note: 1360: the Treaty of Brétigny, ratified at Calais on 24 October 1360, hands Edward III an enlarged Aquitaine. The lands listed: 'Guyenne, Gascony, Poitou, Saintonge, Aunis, Agenais, Périgord, Limousin, Quercy, Bigorre, Gauré, Angoumois, Rouergue' (with Calais, Ponthieu and Guînes outside the duchy), held 'free and clear, without doing homage'; Edward renounced the French crown. The page dates the drafting to 8 or 10 May 1360 and the ratification to 24 October.

1362: Edward III makes the Black Prince Prince of Aquitaine. 'In 1362, Edward III, as Lord of Aquitaine, made his eldest son' Prince of Aquitaine: the duchy becomes the Principality of Aquitaine, the same state and colour. The Brétigny treaty replaced the title 'duke of Aquitaine' by 'lord of Aquitaine'.

ledger.note: 1377: the Brétigny lands beyond Gascony and the Bordelais are back with the French crown (restored 'to its 13th-century limits' says the Guyenne page; 'around Bordeaux' says the Treaty page, the narrower is drawn).
1390: Richard II appoints John of Gaunt Duke of Aquitaine. 'In 1390, King Richard II' appointed his uncle John of Gaunt, 'and the title passed to Gaunt's descendants'; the duchy stays the same state.

region.text: Guyenne and Gascony, the English duchy around Bordeaux

ledger.note: 1451: Charles VII conquers Guyenne. 'Charles VII conquered Guyenne and finally united it to the French crown' (Guyenne page, 1451); the Duchy page closes the war with the Battle of Castillon in 1453.

region.text: Guyenne and Gascony around Bordeaux

ledger.note: 1453: Castillon ends the contest. 'French victory was complete with the Battle of Castillon of 1453'.

region.text: the English duchy around Bordeaux and Bayonne, annexed by France

ledger.note: 1453: the duchy is annexed to the French crown. Infobox: 'annexed by the Kingdom of France (1453)'; 'Aquitaine returned to direct royal rule' after Castillon. The Guyenne page adds that Louis XI gave Guyenne to his brother Charles in 1469 and that it returned to the royal domain in 1472.

wars.name: Siege of Barbastro
wars.outcome: William VIII led the allied army that helped Ramiro I of Aragon take the city, killing and enslaving its inhabitants; Aragon lost it again in the following years. No Aquitanian territory changed.
wars.note: Listed to show it was considered; the page names the allied army, the Muslim defenders are not named.

wars.name: Saintonge War

zones.text: Taillebourg ('On 20 July, the French army arrived at Taillebourg') and Saintes ('On 22 or 23 July the French army laid siege to the city of Saintes')

wars.outcome: French victory (infobox); the page has Henry III forced to ask for a five-year truce and a truce signed at Pons on 1 August, both without a year, and no territorial change; Raymond (of Toulouse) was forced to give up Narbonne and Albi.
wars.note: The page names the Kingdom of England, the Earldom of Cornwall, La Marche and Toulouse against France and Poitou (Alphonse); the duchy is listed because Henry III held it (Gascony page: the English kings held the title of Duke of Gascony after 1204), not because the page names it. The war began at Christmas 1241 and in January 1242 (5 January: Alphonse called the Poitevin nobles). Ledger: no event, no land changed hands on the page.

wars.name: Gascon War

zones.text: the duchy of Aquitaine, occupied by France from 1294 ('France then occupied Aquitaine') until the treaty of 20 May 1303

wars.outcome: Philip IV's Parlement declared the fief forfeit on 19 May 1294 and France occupied it; Edward I renounced his vassalage on 24 June 1294; the Treaty of Paris of 20 May 1303 returned the duchy to Edward in exchange for homage.
wars.note: The page names no town taken; Charles of Valois conquered much of the duchy (page). Ledger: occupation_start 1294, occupation_end 1303 (counterpart kingdom-of-france).

wars.name: War of Saint-Sardos

zones.text: the duchy beyond the Gascon core, overrun by Charles of Valois from August 1324 (La Réole surrendered on 22 September)

wars.outcome: French victory (infobox). Montpezat razed, most towns surrendered, La Réole fell on 22 September 1324; the truce of 31 March 1325 left the French their conquests and 'involved the tacit recognition of the loss of most of the duchy'.
wars.note: Cause: the raid on Saint-Sardos on the night after 15 October 1323 (royal sergeant hanged). Ledger: loss of Limousin, Périgord, Quercy and the Agenais to kingdom-of-france, September 1324 (the reading of the lost land is the researcher's, confidence 2).

wars.name: Hundred Years' War
wars.outcome: Philip VI reclaimed the fief in 1337; Brétigny (1360) enlarged the English duchy; war resumed in 1369 and the English were pushed back round Bordeaux by 1377; Castillon (1453) ended English rule.
wars.note: Only the Aquitaine front is listed; the northern campaigns belong to kingdom-of-england and kingdom-of-france. The pages opened date no campaign in 1337-1359, so no contest zone is drawn for those years.

certainty.note: Feudal frontiers of the High Middle Ages, drawn from regions; no page gives a boundary line.
The Treaty of Paris (4 December 1259) and the Treaty of Amiens (1279) fix the duchy by named provinces and cities; the lines inside them stay approximate.
The 1324 loss rests on the War of Saint-Sardos and the truce of 31 March 1325, which name no provinces; the front of 1337-1359 is not dated on the pages.
The Treaty of Brétigny (1360) fixes the duchy by named provinces; the lines inside them stay approximate.
The frontier moves with the war of 1369-1377 and the French conquest of 1451-1453.

notes:
Modelling choice: the duchy has no shape of its own in 1138/1139-1203. Cliopatria draws the land as Kingdom of France in 1139-1151 (163.6k km2, bbox 2.2 W to 4.4 E, 42.7 to 50.6 N) and as Angevin Empire from 1152 (205.8k km2), and the pages agree on the holders (Louis VII by marriage 1137, Henry II by marriage 18 May 1152). The ledger records the 1137 loss to kingdom-of-france and the 1204 return from angevin-empire; the 1152 hand-over from France to Henry belongs to the angevin-empire dossier (eu-11) as a gain from kingdom-of-france. A reviewer who prefers the duchy as a continuing state in personal union can add a keyframe 1139-1203 equal to Cliopatria's 1111 shape.
Cliopatria's 1206-1439 outline (about 9,600 km2 in the Corrèze and eastern Dordogne) is wrong for the English duchy; seven shapes are marked wrong and replaced by new keyframes (1204, 1259, 1279, 1324, 1360, 1369). Cliopatria also keeps the Angevin Empire in 1206-1209 with a bbox to 42.7 N (Gascony), which overlaps the 1204 return in this ledger: eu-11 should end the Angevin hold on Gascony in 1204.
Not modelled: the nominal French occupation that the truce of 31 March 1325 allowed over 'what was left of the Duchy of Aquitaine' (the War of Saint-Sardos page gives no end for it); the 1337-1359 war front (no campaign dated on the pages opened); Rouergue within Guyenne after 1259 (Guyenne page yes, Treaty page silent); the extent of Saintonge ceded in 1259 (extent not on the page); the 1469-1472 French Duchy of Guyenne (Duchy of Guyenne page: Louis XI gave it to his brother Charles; back to the royal domain 1472); the Aquitaine-Toulouse quarrel after 1122. Page conflicts: confiscation of the fief in 1294 (Gascon War page, 19 May) or 1296 (Guyenne page; the dated war page followed); the periphery lost in 1324 (Saint-Sardos page; followed) or 1337 (Duchy page, 'essentially corresponding to Gascony'); Gascony joined in 1053 (Duchy page; followed) or 1058 (William VIII page, followed by duchy-of-gascony /ledger/9).
Vassalage is now in this ledger as well as in kingdom-of-france (counterpart kingdom-of-france, Aquitaine the vassal): 990 (William V page: Robert II is his 'suzerain'), ended 1137 (Duchy page; France has 1138), again from 4 December 1259 (Treaty of Paris page: 'a vassal to Louis') to 1337 (Duchy page: Philip VI 'reclaimed the fief'; France has May 1337). The Gascon War page has Edward I renouncing vassalage on 24 June 1294 and the treaty of 20 May 1303 returning the duchy for homage; the span is kept whole with the 1294-1303 occupation laid over it. 1360: the Brétigny lands are held 'without doing homage', so no vassal event.
Gazetteer names needed: Loudun, Mirebeau, Confolens, Ruffec, Chabanais (places). Counterpart without dossier: County of Angoulême (Confolens, Ruffec, Chabanais, 1030). The Principality of Aquitaine page returned the Duchy article, so it is listed as a page opened but adds nothing. The Duchy of Aquitaine infobox gives no area, so the area check is by text only.
Double drawing (open question for the orchestrator): Cliopatria's Kingdom of England shapes of 1210-1458 hold English Gascony (south edge 42.69 N in 1210-1384, 43.28 N in 1385-1458; kingdom-of-england_1363 is 286,021 km2 with the Brétigny lands), and the kingdom-of-france dossier takes these lands from kingdom-of-england (1360 loss, 1369 contest, 1380 gain, 1451-1453). The keyframes _1204 to _1369 of this dossier draw the same land as duchy-of-aquitaine, so it is drawn twice until one dossier is chosen. If this dossier keeps it, eu-11 subtracts it from kingdom-of-england and eu-10 renames France's counterparts for 1360, 1369, 1380 and 1451-1453 to duchy-of-aquitaine; if kingdom-of-england keeps it, the keyframes of this dossier for 1204-1453 become the English-held part of that state and the ledger events of 1204, 1259, 1279, 1324, 1360-1377 and 1451-1453 move with it.
Saintonge before 1062: the County of Anjou page has Saintonge as Fulk's appanage until 1062 (ledger gain 1062), but Cliopatria's Duchy of Aquitaine shapes already hold 27 of 29 cells of Charente-Maritime from 990. The shapes are kept; the map shows no change in 1062. | fx-32 F215: every region 'Limousin' in the keyframes and ledger from 1259 (keyframes _1259, _1279 and the two later ones, ledger 11, 12, 14-16, 18, 20-22) is now the Limousin less La Marche; the war zone lists keep the plain region.
